transcript:
## Q1 — WHAT IS IT MADE OF

**Q1_A:** I cannot tell. Flat mid-grey above, near-black below. If forced: "painted concrete kerb." Not stone, not brick, not anything you could name by touch.

**Q1_B:** Mortared stone blockwork — irregular quarried blocks, two courses visible in the face, deep recessed joints. You'd put a hand on cold rough stone.

**Q1_WHY_A:** I sampled every wall-top pixel in the image (grey, 70<v<120, low saturation — 54,663 px). **86.7% of them are the single value (90,90,90).** 7.2% more is the seam grid (71,71,71), 4.5% is the north-edge highlight (107,101,95). 98.4% of the entire standing surface of this map is three flat RGB values. A 96×48 patch of wall top at (432,312)–(528,360) contains **8 unique colours in 4,608 pixels.** There is no material there to name — there is a fill and a grid.

**Q1_WHY_B:** The face band at y 170–202 (crop shown at 6× from (230,168)) is two courses of blocks of genuinely varying width — ~14 px, ~28 px, ~50 px — set in a 2 px dark mortar joint, with the coursing broken rather than regular. The bottom 2–3 px of that band is a dappled alternating light/dark row where the wall meets the ground: erosion at the base. That's mortared rubble-course masonry and it reads as such.

## Q2 — SOLID MASS OR FLAT PATTERN

**Q2_A: Solid mass — the grammar is stated, but the mass is hollow.** Every grey run carries a 48 px light top and a 24 px dark face on its south side only, and it returns that face at wall ends (the vertical run at x 216–264 terminates at y 208 with a full face across its width at y 208–232). The projection is correct and unambiguous. But the mass is asserted by geometry alone — the top surface it's asserting is a flat fill. It reads as a solid box wrapped in blank paper.

**Q2_B: Solid mass, and it proves it.** The decider is not the room boundary — it's the free-standing stub at **(183,393)–(250,466)**, out in the middle of the floor. It carries the identical top-plus-face treatment as the north wall: top y 395–427, hard seam, face y 430–462. A recolour of the room's edge cannot produce a detached block in the middle of the room that obeys the same rule. The west wall does it too: it runs x 0–55 down to y≈425 and stops with a proper returned brick face at y 427–458, floor continuing past it.

## Q3 — WHERE THE GROUND STOPS

**Q3_A:** At the bottom wall, the ground ends at **y = 360** across the full width. Above it: nothing — the grey top (y 312–360) already replaced the ground at y=312 with a hard 1 px edge plus a 3 px light highlight (107,101,95) at y 309–312. Below y=360: a 24 px black band, three courses of 12×8 bricks. **The whole transition is 1 pixel.** One row of grey, next row of black. No crumbling, no debris, no ambiguity, no interest.

**Q3_B:** At the north wall, ground ends at **y = 202**, x 60–366 and x 430–700. Across it: a 2–3 px dappled row of alternating light and dark pixels — the base of the wall breaking up into the floor — then 32 px of brick face (y 170–202), then a hard 2 px black seam at y 170, then the wall top. **Roughly 4 px of transition, then 32 px of stated thickness.** The dappled row is the only place in either picture where a wall admits to having a bottom.

## Q4 — WHAT HOLDS IT TOGETHER

**Q4_A: NOTHING.** One candidate: the timber ladder at **(228,216)–(240,260)**, orange rungs across the wall face at x 216–264, running down onto the floor. It is leaning on the wall, not holding it. Cut it and a ladder falls over. The doors at (68,145)–(118,195) hang in openings; the mortar is drawn but is a 1 px seam that carries nothing. Four hundred years of rope, pins, hide and salvaged timber, and there is not one pin in this image.

**Q4_B: NOTHING.** One candidate: the object at **(135,131)–(147,170)** in the north wall top — a vertical shaft with three horizontal rungs, driven down into the wall's edge. A ladder, or a pin with washers; I cannot tell which, and it is invisible at native lighting. Cut it and nothing moves. Everything else stands by mortar alone. Same failure as A, one notch less total.

## Q5 — BUILT OR REPEATED

**Q5_A: REPEATED, and I can prove it.** I hashed the bottom wall as 24×24 tiles. Across 46 wall-top tiles there are **16 distinct tiles, and one of them occurs 10 times, another 9** — byte-identical, not similar. Across the 23-tile face band there are **4 distinct tiles total**, two of which cover 19 of the 23. Horizontal autocorrelation of the face band (y 360–384) peaks at lag 96 (r=0.54), 48 (0.51), 72, 120, 24 — the full harmonic ladder of a 24 px stamp. This is a tileset being laid down, and it does not disguise it.

**Q5_B: BUILT.** Autocorrelation of the north wall face (y 172–202) shows **no periodicity at any lag from 8 to 140** — the strongest peaks are at lag 8–22, which is block scale, i.e. adjacent-block correlation, not a repeat. The blocks are different widths, the coursing wanders, the joint pattern doesn't close. One exception, in Q8.

## Q6 — WOULD IT SHIP

**Q6_A: YES** — it would ship. It is not good. It is not even competent at the thing being judged: the walls are a placeholder grey that got a grid and shipped. Competent at the *system* (correct projection, correct returns, working doors); blank at the *material*.

**Q6_B: YES.** And on the face band — the one surface actually lit — it is **genuinely good**. Irregular bond, real joints, an eroded base, and a free-standing stub that keeps the rule. That is drawn, not generated. The rest of it is not good, it's just dark.

## Q7 — WHAT'S LEGIBLE AT 1:1

**Q7_A — legible at 1:1, no zoom:** the 24 px seam grid; the 3 px light highlight along every wall's north edge; the green mould, which is the only thing with any presence on these walls; the face band as *a black bar* — you can tell it's darker, you cannot resolve courses. **Blank at 1:1:** the brick coursing in the face, the 1 px speckles (5–8 per tile), the hairline cracks, the tan drip marks under the bricks, the two lighter patch-bricks. **Does not change with distance** — A has no falloff, so the wall at x=550 is as legible as the wall at x=90, and both are a grey rectangle.

**Q7_B — legible at 1:1, no zoom:** the brick coursing and mortar joints of the north face band across roughly **x 180–560** — you can count courses and see individual blocks of different widths without zooming; the corridor mouth as a gap in that band; the stub at (183,393)–(250,466) as a distinct standing object. **Blank at 1:1:** the entire north wall top (y 0–170), the entire south wall top (y 715–800), the west wall (x 0–55) — all functionally black; the ladder at (135,131); the eroded base row. **Changes sharply with distance:** legibility of the face band dies past roughly 200 px from the figure at (390–430, 400–460) — at x<180 and x>560 the same band is black.

**Q7_WHY:** Checked at 1:1 — A: (0,300)–(576,390) and (0,110)–(290,200). B: (60,150)–(540,215) and (60,700)–(540,780). Had to magnify — A: (432,312)–(528,360) at 8×, (300,356)–(420,388) at 8×, (25,356)–(80,384) at 10×. B: (230,168)–(400,206) at 6×, (150,60)–(320,170) at 6× with gamma lift, (115,120)–(165,180) at 10× with gamma lift, (250,712)–(420,800) at 6× with gamma lift. Anything I only found via gamma lift I am counting as hunting, not seeing.

## Q8 — WHAT MY EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO

**Q8_A:** Three things.
1. **The 24 px grid.** It is a perfect square lattice, identical everywhere, and it never once corresponds to a block edge in the face band below it. The top of the wall and the front of the wall are two unrelated patterns stacked.
2. **The patch-brick.** A single lighter brick with a grey top edge at **(37,368)–(59,378)** and again, pixel-identical, at **(370,368)–(392,378)**. Twice in one wall.
3. **The green mould.** Every blob is on the vertical run, x 218–257, from y 147 to y 330, plus one at (330,312). It is one asset placed four times down one column of the map and nowhere else.

**Q8_B:** Yes — **the south wall top, y 720–800, x 60–700.** Horizontal autocorrelation peaks at **lag 64 px (r=0.60)** with its harmonic at 128. A 2-tile stamp — wide block, narrow block, soft blotch — running the entire width of the picture. In the flat-fielded view you can count the cycles. In native lighting it's in the dark and costs nothing on screen, but it is there.

## Q9 — WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS

**Q9_A: Another lit room, at the same value, visible over the top.** There is no "beyond" in this frame. Every wall is a 72 px strip with more brown floor on its far side — I can see over all of them. The black below y=390 is letterbox, not fiction. What the image tells me: the map is entirely revealed, so the walls function as dividers you look across rather than as anything that hides. I am not scoring this — it follows from the even lighting I was told not to penalise.

**Q9_B: More of the same stone, going on past where the light reaches.** Not empty, not another room, not unnameable — continuous. What told me: the wall-top blockwork at (60,20)–(300,165) keeps producing new block edges all the way to the image border with no boundary and no falloff in structure, only in light; and the east side (x 640–750) is the *same worked floor* running off the frame with diagonal tool-hatching and pecked strike-marks still legible under gamma lift. The room does not end where the light does. That is the correct answer for a place in continuous heavy use.

## Q10 — THE GAP NORTH OF THE FIGURE

**Q10_A:** Found it — the doorway at **(68,145)–(118,195)**, directly north of the orc at (95,250). **I read it as a passage**, but only because someone hung a door in it: a timber leaf with an orange arch lintel and two iron ring pulls. Take the door away and it is a notch — the grey stops at x=68 with a dead-straight vertical cut, the black band stops at the same x with another dead-straight cut, and 48 px of ordinary floor runs through 72 px of "solid wall" with no jamb, no reveal, no returned edge. The prop is carrying the read, not the structure.

**Q10_B:** Found it — the corridor at **x 366–430, running north from y 202 to y 0** (64 px, two tiles). **I read it as a passage.** What made the difference: the face band terminates cleanly on both jambs and the *floor material continues north up the channel*, hatching and all, getting darker with distance rather than stopping. A notch would have the wall's own top surface in the gap. This one has floor in it, receding. I could commit to walking into it without testing.

## Q11 — HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED

**Q11_A: Almost nothing, and the little that did happen is decals.** Read from: 5–8 stray 1 px dots per 24×24 tile; three hairline cracks, at (220,123)–(253,140), (231,10)–(263,23), and one on the bottom wall; four mould blobs, all in one column; small tan drips under the face bricks; two identical patch-bricks. Against a flat (90,90,90) field this reads as a clean surface someone flicked dirt at last week. Nothing has *happened* to this wall. Nothing has worn it, loaded it, cracked it under load, or been repaired into it.

**Q11_B: Worn at the base and nowhere else.** Read from: the 2–3 px dappled erosion row along the whole wall/floor junction at y≈200; the broken, non-repeating coursing, which reads as stone laid and re-laid rather than run in one go; the ladder driven into the north wall top at (135,131). But the wall *tops* — more than half the visible standing surface — carry no incident at all: 46–56 distinct values across 34,800 px at (60,20)–(300,165), all inside RGB 8–12, block-scale tonal blocking and nothing else. No cracks, no patches, no rope, no pins, no timber. The four-hundred-year garrison has not touched this wall either.

## CULL

**CULL_A:** Wall surface is 87% one flat grey plus a grid; provably stamped — 4 tiles build a 23-tile wall.

**CULL_B:** Wall tops carry zero texture — the lit stub at (183,393) is flat bars beside densely worked floor.

## RANK

**RANK: B**

B's walls are demonstrably built: no periodicity in the north face, irregular bond, an eroded base, a returned face where the west wall terminates at y≈425, and a detached stub in mid-floor that obeys the same top/face rule — which is the one thing a flat border pattern cannot fake. A's walls are demonstrably stamped, and I mean that literally: byte-identical 24 px tiles, one of them ten times in a single run, over a field where 98.4% of pixels are three RGB values. A has the better *system* — correct returns everywhere, working doors, an unmistakable read of thickness at any distance. B has the better *wall*. Both fail Q4 identically: nothing in either picture is holding anything up, in a fiction whose entire premise is four centuries of visible repair.

## FLIP LIST — A

- Replace the (90,90,90) wall-top fill with actual coursed blockwork of varying size; break the 24 px square lattice so the top's joints relate to the face's joints below.
- Build the face band from at least 12 distinct 24 px tiles with irregular brick widths — 4 tiles for a 23-tile wall is visible as a beat.
- Cut a returned reveal into the door opening at (68,145)–(118,195) so the wall shows its 72 px depth at the jambs instead of ending in a straight vertical slice.
- Add load-bearing repair to the standing surfaces: driven pins, lashed rope, salvaged timber let into the face — at least one per wall run, not one ladder in the whole map.
- Stop placing the mould asset only on x 218–257; it currently marks one column of the map and reads as a stamp, not as damp.

## FLIP LIST — B

- Texture the wall tops. The stub at (183,393)–(250,466) sits in the brightest light in the frame and is five flat bars beside a floor that is dense with hatching and pecking — that contrast is the picture's worst moment.
- Break the 64 px repeat along the south wall top (y 720–800, r=0.60 at lag 64); vary the block widths as the north face already does.
- Add visible repair to the face band — pins, rope, a timber prop let into the courses — so the wall shows the garrison, not just age.
- Carry the eroded base row (currently only at y≈200) around the west wall's returned face at y 427–458 and the stub's face at y 430–462, so every wall foot behaves the same way.
- Give the corridor jambs at x 366 and x 430 a distinct wear signature at floor level, so a passage reads as *used* and not merely open.
